REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JUNE 28   RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Yesterday a rather acrimonious debate took place in this house on a subject I do not think I need mention, since I am sure it is still fresh in the minds of many hon. members; and I am hopeful, of course, that it will not be revived today. During the course of the debate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) used the word "cowardly" with respect to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and the Prime Minister demanded that the word should be withdrawn. I ruled that the word was unparliamentary, and that the leader of the opposition must withdraw it.
In reply the leader of the opposition stated that the Prime Minister had charged him with lack of courage. I did not recall having heard the Prime Minister use the words, and accordingly did not order him to withdraw them. The leader of the opposition insisted that the words had been used, and the Prime Minister stated that if he had used the words he would withdraw them. Apparently the house has left it to me to determine whether the words complained of by the leader of the opposition were used by the Prime Minister.
I have read in Hansard the record of the proceedings in the house yesterday, and I cannot find that the words referred to by the leader of the opposition were used. Accordingly I rule that the Prime Minister did not use the words "lack of courage", and that a withdrawal is not necessary. I further rule that as the leader of the opposition did use the word "cowardly" it is necessary that he withdraw it. In closing his remarks the leader of the opposition said:
If the Prime Minister used words different from those which I heard, and which I think I heard correctly, then obviously my remarks were related to words which were not said. Hansard will speak for itself.
I draw the attention of hon. members to these words:
If they were not said, then I withdraw what I said in relation to them.
Accordingly I accept the withdrawal of the leader of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of reviving the discussion. I would simply point out that if you will check the record carefully you will see that what I referred to was the implication of the words. I also have checked the Hansard record; and I need not remind you that an implication has the same result as a direct statement.
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): I do not wish to revive the debate, either, but I do wish to point out the impression that seems to have been left with objective newspapermen in reporting it. The inference or impression left with reputable newspapermen who were attempting, I think, to give an objective report, is to be found in the report in the Montreal Gazette of today, the last part of which is as follows:
Mr. St. Laurent jumped to his feet.
"Mr. Speaker," he said, "may I through you ask ' the leader of the opposition if we are to take this merely more or less as a successful attempt to retire behind a smoke screen, or if he does in a manly way take the responsibility of asserting any charge whatsoever on the floor of this house."
Mr. Drew snapped:
"Mr. Speaker, I do net take very kindly to the inference by the Prime Minister that I am not acting with proper courage, but I do not think that my remarks indicate that I am as cowardly as the Prime Minister, acting in the way he has in regard to a minister with the power this minister has."
At that point, Mr. St. Laurent demanded the immediate withdrawal of the word "cowardly." Speaker Ross Macdonald agreed the word was unparliamentary and ordered Mr. Drew to withdraw.
The Progressive Conservative leader, amid a swelling hubbub, refused to relent unless Mr. St. Laurent withdraw what he understood to be the words "lack of courage."
Mr. St. Laurent said he had not used that phrase; he thought he had used the words "manly course." If the official record proved him wrong, he would withdraw.
Mr. Drew said he, too, would let the record speak for itself, and the matter rested there.
If that is the impression that has been left, the matter cannot rest there. I do not mind what epithets the leader of the opposition may choose to apply to me, or how much vilification he may attempt to heap upon me. But when unparliamentary language is used in this house and the Speaker of the house orders the member using it to withdraw it, it does not matter who he is; whether he is Prime Minister, Leader of the Opposition, or anyone else, he must comply with the order of the Speaker, and the matter cannot rest until he has done

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH GOVERNMENT OF HONG KONG-EXEMPTIONS FROM PROVISIONS OF SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I answer the question .put to me yesterday by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) about the dates of the exemption from certain regulations of the ships of the Ming Sung company. The return to the order shows that the exemption in Canada was made on May 16, and was notified to the trade commissioner on May 16, 1950. The correspondence dealing with that is in the return. I added verbally that doubts had been raised subsequently as to the sufficiency of that exemption, in view of the terms of the shipping regulations of 1899 of the government of Hong Kong, and that, at the request of the Canadian government, the government of the United Kingdom had had exemption under those regulations issued subsequently.
The doubt was first expressed in a confidential letter from a law officer of the government of Hong Kong to our trade commissioner on October 13, 1950. The regulations of Hong Kong were amended either on January 4 or January 5, 1951, and then on January 5, 1951, that exemption from those orders was issued by the Hong Kong administration.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that we hope this may be the last day of the session, I am wondering whether the Prime Minister feels that it would be in the public interest to bring the house up to date with respect to the proposed negotiations in connection with peace in Korea and the part that Canada is playing in it. I make that suggestion because of the keen interest all hon. members have in this very important matter. I am quite sure that if the Prime Minister has a statement he feels he could make at the moment, the house would be pleased to hear it.
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): I am sorry; I have no information that has not already been published in the Canadian and United Stales press. The hon. member and the people of Canada can be assured that Canada will do everything within its power to bring about a cease-fire, for which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has been working incessantly for many months.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister one other question relating to the same subject? Who is representing Canada in the negotiations which are in progress at the present time among the other United Nations who are interested in the Korean campaign?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext:
It is difficult to give a
categorical answer, because there are talks going on in many different places. The Secretary of State for External Affairs himself has been in close touch with the foreign secretary in London, our ambassador in in close touch with the state department at Washington. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, either today or tomorrow, will be proceeding to Oslo, and intends to visit other foreign ministers in western Europe. He had an interview with Mr. Trygve Lie at one of the airports; and the matter is of course being discussed at the headquarters of the United Nations by our acting permanent delegate there at the present time Mr. John Holmes. Herbert Norman also arrived there yesterday, or is arriving there today
The matter is one which is of such interest to all those who have participated in the

United Nations actions in Korea that it is being discussed where any of them can make contacts.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE

subtopic: DEVIL'S HOLE ON RIDEAU RIVER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DEVIL'S HOLE ON RIDEAU RIVER
subsubtopic: QUESTION AS TO ACTION TO PREVENT FURTHER LOSS OF LIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask
Inquiries of the Ministry a question of the Minister of Public Works, of which I have given oral notice. I realize that to some extent my question will be only by way of notice, but I wished to bring the minister's attention to the matter before the session closes.
As all hon. members are aware, particularly those living in or near Ottawa, a short time ago, at the place known as Devil's Hole, at Hog's Back on the Rideau river, a fine young lad of twenty, Gerald Fink, a superb athlete, lost his life. In view of the fact that there have been other tragedies at that point, I took the matter up and had inquiries made through the municipal council, the federal district commission and the Rideau canal offices of the Department of Transport, as well as at the office of the chief engineer of the Department of Public Works. It seemed impossible to get any definite assurance as to which body has authority, or as to which of those official organizations had control over that particular spot.
After the recent tragedy, the father of the young man, Dr. Fink, seemed mostly concerned about the possibility of the same thing happening to anyone else. With this in our minds I think every effort should be made to bring together the various authorities with a view to seeing whether there is some way of preventing the use of waters in which, as has been demonstrated, it is extremely dangerous to dive or swim.
I bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, because his department has control over all navigable waters, and this is part of a navigable stream; therefore there should be some measure of jurisdiction under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I hope he will take appropriate steps to bring the various authorities together with a view to seeing whether something can be done to prevent swimming at that particular place in the river.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates for the customs and excise divisions of the national revenue department are made up of five votes totalling $23,790,574. Of this total amount, salaries for the staff comprise 82-75 per cent. In addition to the main estimates there is a supplementary item of $138,700, vote No. 735.
This division is responsible for the collection of customs and excise duties and taxes.
(Mr. Fournier (Hull).]
These revenues, and the work entailed in collecting them, rose in 1950-51 to $1,256,000,000, exceeding 1949-50 by $203,000,000. The budget speech delivered by my colleague the Minister of Finance forecast customs and excise revenues for 1951-52 of $1,487,000,000, which is an increase of $231,000,000 over last year. The revenues for April and May are running well ahead of last year.
There are many different aspects and functions in the work of the customs and excise divisions. However, perhaps the most significant single yardstick for measuring the volume of work in these divisions is the number of import entries. In 1950-51 this figure rose more than eight per cent over the previous year, and the preliminary reports for the first two months in this fiscal year show an increase in work of more than seventeen per cent over the corresponding months last year.
With regard to tourist traffic, figures for the first five months in 1951 indicate an increase of more than six per cent over last year in the number of automobiles entering Canada, and there is an increase of more than ten per cent in the number of people entering Canada other than by automobile.
All these things mean a greater volume of business, especially at border points. However, I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that despite the increasing work load I have mentioned, the customs-excise estimates for 1951-52, taking all five votes together, provide for practically no increase in staff over the previous year.
Obviously if we are to handle more work with the same staff it is necessary to increase efficiency of operations. One measure has been the merging of primary customs and immigration examination of travellers at frontier points. This program has been in progress for several months, and is being extended as rapidly as possible. We hope that the savings in manpower in my department and the citizenship and immigration department will be significant.
Another efficiency measure has been the improvement of internal procedures in our field offices and at headquarters. Every effort is being made to streamline our procedures and to handle the increased volume of work without adding to the staff.
Finally, I should point out that the maintaining of small customs-excise offices, employing only one or two men, is an expensive business, both in money and in manpower.
The first item to be voted is No. 309, general administration, amounting to $1,936,980. This vote represents the cost of maintaining the headquarters administration of the Customs

Act, the Customs Tariff, the Excise Tax Act, and the Excise Act, together with regulations established under these statutes. In addition to the administering of these statutes, the customs-excise division administers, in part, on behalf of other departments, approximately forty other acts, such as the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the Copyright Act, the Foreign Exchange Control Act, etc., and regulations relating thereto.

Last year when we were
dealing with a similar item in the minister's estimates I raised a question with regard to the holding of sales in Toronto of goods seized for non-payment of customs and excise duties, and I should like to raise it again today. What I said last year is to be found at page 4300 of Hansard of June 28, 1950, where I am reported as follows:
There is a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, if indeed it has not already been brought to his attention. It has to do with the customs service for the city of Toronto, and the methods now followed of selling goods that have been placed under seizure. According to my information the methods now being followed are not efficient, and are not yielding the full value that could be realized on the sale of goods. There was a time when goods were sold at auction by true auctioneers who gave adequate publicity to the sale. According to my present information that method was abandoned some time ago as a result of some patronage difficulties that the government encountered, and now the sales are simply carried through by members of the staff of the department who are not qualified as auctioneers.
Here is a situation where more money could be yielded to the public treasury if efficient methods were followed in realizing the utmost possible on
Supply-National Revenue goods under seizure. I would ask the minister to look into this matter, and give it his personal attention because, according to the information I have, much more could be realized on the sales if efficient auctioneering methods were followed.
The minister replied as follows:
I had not any knowledge that the method of disposal of seized goods had been changed. Notice of the auction is given to the public press and the goods are sold by auction. It may well be that there is a difference in the classes of auctioneers. Some auctioneers may be able to get a better price for goods than others, but the best possible price is realized when goods under seizure are disposed of. However I shall be glad to look into the suggestions of the hon. member for Eglinton, and if the method is not up to date we shall bring it up to date.
According to my information, the steps that have been taken to bring the methods up to date and to make them efficient have been entirely inadequate. According to the information which I have, sales which are held under the auspices of the department have been carried on with the minimum of advertising in the press and are not conducted by trained auctioneers. Under such circumstances it is inevitable that much less is realized from the sale of seized goods than might be realized if efficient methods were followed.
Formerly these sales were conducted by auctioneers who did considerable advertising and endeavoured to bid up prices in an effort to realize the utmost possible from the sale of goods. I am told that the government ran into some patronage problems in connection with the auctioneers, and there seemed to be some rivalry for the governmental largesse, so the government decided to dispense with the services of auctioneers. Whatever the government's difficulties may be in distributing its largesse, the fact of the matter is if they are simply going to use the services of people in the department who have no particular training in auctioneering, less is going to be realized on the sale of these goods than could be realized by the use of the services of someone trained in auctioneering goods.
I was given one example of a new article that was sold at a sale in Toronto about a month ago. I am told it was worth approximately $1,800, and on the sale something like $500 was realized. I was told by a person who attended the sale, having seen a little squib of an advertisement in the paper beforehand, or I think the notice at the dominion building in Toronto, that the article was valuable, and that if an attempt had been made to advertise the sale and to use the services of an efficient auctioneer to have the article bid up, a substantially larger sum could have been realized.
Just a few days after that sale I am told that another sale was held in Toronto, the department on that occasion using the services of an auctioneer. If they saw fit in the

Supply-National Revenue case of the latter sale to retain the services of an auctioneer, I am more surprised that they did not on the earlier occasion, because the two occasions were separated by a matter of only a few days, I think less than two weeks; and a substantial loss resulted on the first occasion from inadequate prices realized because of not following efficient methods of sale. I hope that the use of an auctioneer on the occasion of the latter sale marks a departure in policy on the part of the government, and that we may be assured that from this time on steps will be taken to retain the services of efficient auctioneers and to give adequate publicity to the sales so that the best possible prices may be realized on the sale of seized goods.

I should like to pass on a suggestion which I think might help the minister to obtain the results he outlined to us, more efficiency and better work from the people in his department. I have occasion to cross and recross the United States boundary at different times in the year, and almost every year. I have noticed that when I come to a port of entry to return to Canada, often the officials are very busy. At times there may be two or three dozen people waiting to make a declaration of articles that they have acquired in the United States. As a rule when busses or cars discharge their passengers at the customs house, they will go to the desk and the officials will quickly distribute the appropriate form; I think it is E-24. The travellers are required to list the articles they have brought across. When they are finished and have signed their declarations, the government official has to pick up the forms, and in many instances I have noticed that he has to go back and classify the articles that have been declared. That takes a good deal of his time and holds up the whole crowd.
I have wondered if a suggestion of this kind could not be carried out; it would not cost very much, and I feel that it would help both the customs officials and the travelling public. You might print right on the face of the form the various headings under which the customs officer reports back to headquarters. For instance, the first heading I have noticed is automobile accessories; then automobile tires and tubes; then shoes, ladies', gentlemen's and children's; then clothing, ladies', gentlemen's and children's. It seems to me it would be quite simple to have these classifications printed on the forms. Then when the officials handed them out to the travelling public they would see at once that the articles were supposed to be declared in that order and would do so, and in that way save a good deal of time. For what the suggestion is worth I am bringing it to the attention of the minister.

This item deals with
administration, and I should like to take a moment to outline to the committee and the minister a situation existing in one community of my district, which I think points a moral.
In the community of Atlin in northern British Columbia, entirely by their own efforts an airport was constructed at which for some years foreign aircraft might land and be cleared. According to my information the clearing was done by the postmaster, under some special arrangement, and his fee was a percentage of the fee he collected from those operating the planes. In other words if no planes landed there was no expense to the department. That permission was withdrawn in 1947, effective in 1948. We have no objection to the curtailment of service in the interests of economy, but in this case I submit there was no practical economy. Neither would we have any particular objection in that part of the country to a curtailment of service in the interests of security in time of war, when to have foreign planes landing at isolated places might not be a good idea. But I respectfully submit that in the years since world war II no question of security has been involved, and, so far as I am able to ascertain, no question of economy is involved.
The moral which I think this points, and which I would seriously submit not only to the minister but to the government as a whole, is that where departments of this kind, which I would call service departments as distinct from such departments as public works which are spending departments, can assist the smaller and more isolated communities to develop, even if only in a small way, at practically no expense to the government, very serious consideration should be given to extending that assistance, even though at times it may involve a slight departure from normal routine in the department.

Yes. It has been my practice, in presenting to the house the estimates of the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, to make a brief statement regarding some of the more important aspects of the division's operations.
On page 41 of the estimates will be found the items comprising the requirements of the division. It will be noted that with respect to the administration of the division itself, the estimates have been reduced by $3,816,000 as compared with the estimates for the fiscal year ending March, 1951, and that there is a reduction of $10,000 in respect of the estimates for the income tax appeal board.
At pages 321 to 326 inclusive will be found the details of the various items.
Of the total amount of $25,472,294 requested by the department, some $22,040,694 represents salaries. This compares with a figure of $25,330,550 in the estimates for the previous fiscal year.
When I last reported to the house, I stated that the staff of the department at the end of May, 1950, consisted of 10,477 persons. At that time I indicated that there would be a continuing shrinkage. At the end of May, 1951, the staff had come down to 6,944 people. This, I believe, represents substantially the minimum number that can efficiently maintain the operations. There may be some further reductions due to the release of unsuitable people, but it is my expectation that the total staff will not be less than at

present and may in fact tend to be slightly higher as and when suitable applicants for employment are available.
I should probably repeat that the introduction of new methods and procedures and the bringing of the work to a current basis have been mainly responsible for the material reductions which have been effected. It may interest hon. members to learn that as of the 31st May, 1950, the average monthly salary for the division was $190, whereas at 31st May, 1951, the average monthly salary was $245. This change is partly due to the salary increases recently put into effect, and partly due to the fact that the staff generally is more highly trained and tends to consist of persons in the higher grades. Obviously the reduction in dollar amount on a strictly comparable basis would be substantially greater if the salary scales in effect at present were those in effect in the year ending March, 1950.
At this point I should make brief reference to the volume of work. At the end of May, 1950, there was an inventory of individual returns of 745,868. At the end of May, 1951, this figure was 375,983, although the returns received in the three months ending May 31, 1950 and 1951, were respectively 3,121,800 and 3,314,288.
In respect of corporation returns, the figures are equally interesting. At the end of May, 1950, there were 26,723 returns in hand, whereas at the end of May, 1951, there were 18,887.
From my personal observations, I think it has been generally acknowledged that the public are receiving satisfactory service from the department's officers throughout the country.
The second largest item in the estimates represents printing, stationery, supplies and equipment. These total $1,253,500, compared with $1,605,000 in the estimates of last year. The actual expenditures last year were some $932,000, which represents a substantial reduction. The costs of these materials are continuing to rise, but every effort is being made to effect the most extensive economies possible in the production and distribution of forms.
Unfortunately it is not possible, apparently, to eliminate large waste in the forms supplied to the public through the district offices and the local post offices. The division has made efforts to persuade taxpayers to take only enough forms to serve their individual requirements but, for one reason or another, the consumption appears to represent more than double the theoretical need.

The next large item is travelling expenses. In the estimates this year, this amounts to $792,000 compared with $900,000 in the previous year. The actual expenditures were $620,000. The administration of the taxing legislation requires a great deal of travelling to be done in the field. The expenses themselves are checked with the greatest care by the department and by officers of the treasury. I am satisfied that only necessary travelling is being done and that it is being done at minimum cost.
Postage at $650,000 compares with $700,000 in the estimates for last year, and actual expenditure of some $515,797. This represents the postage account of the district offices only. Mail originating from head office at Ottawa is carried without charge to the department.
Law costs is the only item in respect of which the division is asking for an increased .appropriation. This item for 1951-52 is $253,000, compared with $200,000 in the previous year. The greatly increased number of appeals since the creation of the income tax appeal board and the stepping up of the division's collection program were primarily responsible for the increase in legal costs.
I might comment briefly on some of the other larger items. Telephone and telegraph at $117,000 is substantially the same as last year at $120,000. Advertising is down from $60,000 to $27,000. This covers only the annual "file early" campaign conducted at the beginning of each year for the purpose of advising the public of the filing dates and the accessibility of the necessary forms, and the advantages of getting returns prepared and filed on time.
Bank charges at $57,000 compare with $60,000 last year and represent the payments to the bank in connection with the handling of ownership certificates.
Sundries at $196,700 are slightly down, from $222,000. This covers freight, express, cartage, armoured-car service, overtime meals, distribution of forms, etc.
With respect to the income tax appeal board, there is no important change in the appropriations required. The Hon. Mr. Justice Graham retired as chairman of the board at 31st December, 1950, and was subsequently replaced by Mr. Fabio Monet, K. C., of Montreal. Mr. R. S. W. Fordham, K. C., was added to the board as of April 1, 1951. The board has received since its inception some 750 appeals and has heard 335. Judgments in most of these have been rendered.

Supply-National Revenue
I should like to refer briefly to the collection program which I mentioned in my remarks last year. This program was undertaken to collect all 1949 and prior years' taxes by the end of March, 1951. As of the 15th April, 1951, there was outstanding, over 60 days old, some $11,500,000 in respect of which the division had not been able to effect or arrange for collection, out of a total amount outstanding at that time in respect of assessed returns of $72,600,000.
At the present time, the division is in a position to deal with delinquent taxpayers immediately an assessment has been issued, and it is expected that collections each year will henceforth be maintained on a current basis. Hon. members, I am sure, will agree that this is a highly desirable objective.
In speaking of collection action, I think it is appropriate to mention that overpayments of tax are being refunded to the public with great promptitude. In fact, as of this date, practically all refunds arising out of the filing of 1950 returns have already been made. There are some minor exceptions where the returns themselves could not be accepted, but generally speaking, all refunds, especially to the wage and salary group, are given first priority and are issued with the greatest dispatch. I mentioned this before in dealing with a point that arose when the house was in committee on the 1951 income tax legislation.
Last year I referred to the fact that the department still had on hand some 76,000 cheques payable to individual taxpayers covering refundable savings. At the end of April, 1951, there were still on hand some 67,655 cheques. Every possible effort has been made to find the payees. It is intended to turn the balance of these cheques back to the treasury this month.
Before closing, I should like to deal with .three points which may be of interest to the house. First, the hon. member for Middlesex East made reference in the house recently to :some difficulty that had arisen in his constituency regarding the basic herd. This problem *was dealt with by the department in 1947 and 1948 and, after lengthy discussions with representatives of the farming groups, certain rules were drawn up which seem to be acceptable to and understood by those concerned. These rules were not intended in any way to change the law in the matter, but were prepared to enable farmers to understand where they stood and to help them take the necessary steps to establish their.position.
The rules have been published in the Farmer's Guide, issued by the Department of National Revenue, during each of the last
TMr. McCann.]
three or four years. They have also been set out in many farm journals and have been most widely circulated. The publication of these rules was done to help the farmer. They in no way add to or take away from his legal rights.
Second, it is my intention this year to institute a more vigorous campaign against tax evasion. The department has been successful in uncovering tax dodgers and has collected very large sums of money as a result of its efforts. It is intended to intensify these efforts, and I should like to take this opportunity to warn those persons who have guilty consciences to come forward while they can and straighten out their affairs.
In this regard I should like to direct a particular warning to those who collaborate with tax evaders and who actively assist in the carrying out of schemes of tax fraud. There are few instances in which an important tax fraud can be committed by a taxpayer without the advice and assistance of somebody else. This is a very serious matter, and I am sure the committee will agree with me that every effort should be made to root out those persons and to deal with them vigorously.
Third, the sub-offices at Victoria, British Columbia, Kitchener, Windsor and St. Catharines, Ontario, have been or are being converted into full district offices. At Sudbury suitable space has been acquired, and steps are being taken now to open a sub-office of the Ottawa district office in Sudbury. speechtext:
On June 15, on the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, this item was allowed to stand pending such further information as might be obtained from Hong Kong. Information has been obtained from our trade commissioner in Hong Kong that immediately upon receipt of our inquiry he made a preliminary investigation; that he had read the guild's letter and had communicated with the "Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited (H.K.)"-which

Supply-External Affairs I take it means a company having a Hong Kong charter-as well as with various Hong Kong government officials by telephone, explaining the matter to them and asking for preliminary comment.
The trade commissioner informs us that each of the government officials gave an immediate opinion that so far as he was concerned the charges in the guild's letter seemed fantastic. For example, the director of marine denied absolutely that the vessels were contravening any regulations within his purview. Indeed he said that so far as he was concerned the vessels were the best operated of any based on the harbour, and that there was certainly bias in the opinion expressed by the guild. The personal assistant (trade) to the director of commerce and industry stated that he had never seen any reason to suspect the ships of smuggling gold or anything else, and that to his knowledge the Ming Sung Industrial Company had never been charged with carrying strategic materials whose export was prohibited, or any item for which an export licence had not been issued by the department. Of course the Ming Sung company itself scouted the idea that there was any wrongdoing by their ships.
Then he made inquiries about this so-called Russian captain. There is a captain Peter Francis Hanisch master of the Yen Men. He ascertained that this man was born of mixed parentage in Ningpo, Chekiang province, in 1886, his mother being a Chinese woman and his father a British subject named Joseph Hanisch, employed in the Chinese maritime customs. Both parents are dead, and it is now difficult to get positive verification of these details, but Hanisch had shown our trade commissioner a photostat of his certificate of Chinese naturalization dated April, 1947, issued under the Republic of China Citizenship Act, and the commissioner was quite satisfied that he is a Chinese. He says there is no other person associated with the operation of these ships whom the guild could have had in mind as possibly being a Russian.
With respect to the charges of gold speculation, it may very well be that, as happens very frequently, passengers have been charged with individual smuggling, but there was nothing attributable to the operation of the ships themselves. He examined a recent cargo manifest and found nothing on it that was on the list of the Hong Kong authorities as strategic materials. There were some items for which we require export permits from Canada, but none that was not in the categories that were being traded out of Hong Kong. He states that of course there the situation was rather difficult-balancing
the warehousing trade of the crown colony, which is its means of existence, and the desirability of keeping possible strategic materials away from the Chinese communists. He pointed out what we already knew, that their list of strategic materials was not as extensive as ours and was not as extensive as the United States list, and, as a matter of fact, that the Americans wanted to interrupt all trade of any kind with Hong Kong.

On the whole, I must repeat that, from the very inception of this matter, I have been greatly concerned about it. I have used all possible means to secure information. There may be diverging views as to the propriety of allowing to be performed the operations that were allowed by the crown colony of Hong Kong. There may be those who believe that the policy the United States recommended would have been the preferable policy, namely, to break off trade entirely. But that was not the view we took. We took the view that the United Kingdom authorities, with their long experience in oriental foreign policy, were certainly as well informed as we
Supply-External Affairs could be about the situation, and certainly as careful as we ourselves would be about the security and success of their men and ours operating in Korea, and that there was no requirement that we should attempt to assert that our wisdom and our consideration for the proper safety of our men was greater than theirs.

speechtext:
I appreciate the endeavours the government has made to obtain the additional information on this question which was raised some two weeks ago. I also appreciate the difficulties which exist in obtaining information from Hong Kong. Correspondence takes many weeks to come in the ordinary course of events, and even an air mail letter takes four or five days to come from Hong Kong to Ottawa. Since this question was raised I have received cables, letters, press reports and photographs from Hong Kong, from sources which I have every reason to believe are thoroughly reliable. So far as I know, some of them have no connection whatever with the China coast guild.
Regarding that organization, the Secretary of State for External Affairs on June 15, when this matter was under discussion, asked whether I associated myself with the accuracy of those statements, or their inaccuracy, as he said. I have taken every means at my disposal to find out the degree of reliability and responsibility that might be placed upon the organization known as the China coast guild of navigating and engineer officers. I am pleased to associate myself with that organization to the extent that I believe they are composed of thoroughly responsible officers. They are officers of the merchant marine, and I have no reason whatever to believe that they would attempt to give information which was not to the best of their knowledge absolutely correct. Much of that information has been supported by letters that I have received from other people.
In his remarks the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that I-referring to myself-would not be so happy about the sources of my information when additional information was received by the government. I must take exception to that remark, because the source of my information was in the main the China coast guild, an organization, as I say, of responsible officers of the merchant navy. I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that only a few years ago, during the second war, we were referring to the merchant navy as the fourth arm of the service, and I cannot help thinking that to cast any sort of doubt on the reliability of that organization is an insult to the men who played such a gallant part in the last war.

Supply-External Affairs
As I say, I have taken every step that was possible and open to me, short of going to Hong Kong, which was not practicable, to verify the correctness of their statements. The first statement made in the letter was a description of the routes which were being travelled by these seven ships of the Ming Sung company. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport gave that information. The Minister of Transport on June 21, at page 4412 of Hansard, said:
I have been informed that two vessels, the Lung Men and the Chien Men, are operating between Hong Kong and Macao; two vessels, the Hu Men and Yu Men are laid up at Hong Kong and have been laid up there for the past ten days.
It is quite reasonable to expect that. One must remember that these vessels were originally built for the river trade. The fact that for months they have been trading in the open sea would naturally result in the slackening of their bottoms, which would require extensive repairs. Then he goes on to say:
I am further informed that three vessels, the Shill Men, the Chi Men and the Yen Men, are operating between Hong Kong and Canton but not on a regular service.
That is a little difficult to relate to the statements which appeared in the journal of the Department of Trade and Commerce called Foreign Affairs, where under date of June 1 we are told:
The steamship Chien Men, the Canadian-built river vessel belonging to the Ming Sung Industrial Company, departed on the first trip signalling the resumption of regular passenger service between Hong Kong and Canton. Although the Ming Sung vessels have been running a weekly service to Canton via Macao and ferrying Malayan-Chinese repatriates to the mainland, for several months, this sailing of Chien Men marked the first resumption of direct scheduled Hong Kong-Canton service since the latter port was occupied by the Chinese communists almost two years ago. The new service will operate three times a week, leaving Hong Kong every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.
According to the exemptions dated May 9, contained in sessional paper 124-B and tabled on Wednesday, June 20 of this year, the relaxation is granted to these ships, ships permitted to clear for voyages between Hong Kong and Macao. I call attention to the fact that there is no mention whatever of any relaxation being granted to these ships to trade direct from Hong Kong to Canton. That was the reason I asked the Prime Minister this morning whether there was any further exemption or extension of exemption which would permit the vessels to clear from Hong Kong direct to Canton.
On June 15 the hon. member for Leeds asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if there were ships flying the flags of other nations of United Nations plying on this
[Mr. Pearkes.l
triangular route. I presume that that meant of course the Hong Kong-Macao-Canton route. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said, at page 4198 of Hansard:
To the best of my knowledge there are a great many ships still engaged in the China trade.
The hon. member for Leeds said:
I refer particularly to ships flying the stars and stripes or flags of the commonwealth or of France.
As I say, the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his reply said:
To the best of my knowledge there are a great many ships still engaged in the China trade.
I have made every inquiry that I can, and to the best of my knowledge there are no British ships or United States ships plying into Canton under their own flags. There may be Chinese vessels plying between Hong Kong and Canton, but so far as I can find out-and I have checked with official sources-there are no British or United States vessels flying those flags trading between Hong Kong and Canton. I think that is quite reasonable to assume, because there is an embargo so far as the United States is concerned, and if these vessels did enter a communist port the chances are that they would be seized. I mention that merely to emphasize the uncertainty and difficulty that there sometimes is in getting accurate information.
In pre-war days British-owned vessels did carry passengers and cargo from Hong Kong direct to Canton. As I have said, so far as I know there are no British or United States vessels entering Canton now. The advice I received from Hong Kong is that if they attempted to do so they would be shot at from that point. Therefore all evacuees and cargo going direct from Hong Kong to Canton, such as evacuees or repatriates from Malaya, ' Singapore and Indonesia, would have to travel on these Men vessels, if they went direct from Hong Kong to Canton. As we have been told in the official report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, this repatriation is going on.
I now come to the question of crews. Exemption was granted to this company to employ ships' officers of other than Canadian or British nationality. There was some question about one of those officers, and the information I had concerning one Hanisch corresponds very much with the remarks of the Prime Minister today. He is of mixed parentage, his mother being a Chinese woman. My advice was that his father was an Austrian, while the Prime Minister's advice was that he was a British subject. That is immaterial. He has been a nationalist Chinese. One point which must be noted at this time is that the company has never

stated that these Chinese officers and crews are nationalist Chinese. I suppose that is probably because if they were nationalists they would be arrested on the very next trip they took into Canton. I do not think there is much doubt about that. The only reasonable assumption that can be made is that for purposes of their own safety, these men have acknowledged themselves to be communists in order that they might trade into these communist ports. To suggest otherwise I think would be to avoid facing up to the reality of the situation. In present-day China any resident or inhabitant who is not a communist-well, there is no question about it; it is just a case of being a communist, or else.
The report of May 9 gives as the reason for the exemption that there were no British subjects with certificates of competency available for employment as masters and ships' officers. That is so. But it is rather contradictory, I suggest, to state that we must consider the evidence given by the China coast guild as being biased, presumably because their members want to get those jobs. British or Canadian officers are either available or not available. And if there are no members of the guild available to take over those duties, I do not see why the evidence of the guild should be considered biased.
Now we come to the question of cargo. The Prime Minister has read out a list of certain articles, which corresponds in a general way with some of the information I have. I have information to the effect that steel plate, railway material, ship repairs and lumber have been shipped in pretty considerable quantities. To give a specific example, I understand that on or about June 14 this year, the date on which this question was raised in the house, sixty tons of steel wire was shipped on one of these vessels out of Hong Kong to Canton.
The Prime Minister is reported in the Ottawa Journal as having admitted that limited supplies of scrap iron and rubber tires were shipped from Hong Kong to Red China. I think the information that has been given already this afternoon supports that. I suggest that while it may be possible for a reasonable check to be made on shipments direct from Hong Kong to Canton, no such check can be made on shipments from Macao to Canton. So far as I know, there is no Canadian or even British ambassador or trade commissioner in Macao. The means of checking those shipments would be extremely difficult, and one would have to rely entirely upon Portuguese officials.

I will come to the question of manifests. No doubt shipments which were consigned to Macao in the first place might be reconsigned to Canton without even being unloaded at Macao. To indicate the extent of the trade that there is in commodities which we must say are of essential value, and possibly of considerable strategic value to China, I would quote briefly from a Hong Kong paper this United Press dispatch dated at Macao June 23, under the heading "Frantic rush to beat export ban":
Large amounts of strategic materials are being rushed here from Hong Kong in a last-minute bid to beat the June 25 deadline when the Hong Kong export ban comes into force.
Regular steamers from the British colony are calling here with crammed holds. Cargo space on Macao-bound sailings are fully booked through Sunday and frantic merchants are chartering junks in order to clear out their stocks from Hong Kong before Monday.
The main items involved are machine and automobile spare parts, steel plates, rods and wire.
It will be recalled that in the local papers there was an announcement of a junk having been seized immediately after that. One will note that since that question was raised in the house the British government has seen fit to tighten its regulations regarding exports of materials from Hong Kong. Starting on Tuesday-I believe that was the 25th-there was to be a complete embargo of strategic goods coming out from Hong Kong to China. The Hong Kong government was being requested to set up an import licensing system which would keep out war materials from non-British sources intended for re-export to the Chinese communists.
There is every indication that this unfortunate trade has been going on. While it may be desirable to maintain trade with China, undoubtedly certain sources have abused that privilege, or stretched it to the very limit, and have been sending out materials which are considered of strategic value. I suggest that, while it may be extremely difficult to obtain precise information, a check of the import and export manifests would possibly disclose some of the articles that are being sent. They should disclose all, but the run between Macao and Canton will probably be retained with offices at either Macao or Canton, and it might not be difficult for manifests to disappear, or even for false stamps to be obtained.
I am sure that our trade commissioner in Hong Kong will do his utmost to check and supervise this trade. He is a young man known to me, and I cast no reflections upon his ability. He is in his early thirties, and

Supply-External Affairs had a distinguished record in the last war. He joined the trade commissioner's branch, I think in 1949, but despite his ability and energy undoubtedly he will be lacking in some of the experience necessary to cope with the numerous ramifications of oriental negotiations.
We have had little information about the financial side of the deal. We are told that there are three Canadian banks involved, and that payments are being made now.
I come now to what may be described as the personal side of this unhappy controversy. It will be recalled that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made the statement when replying to me that I should be sorry for having raised this problem.

feel that since the statement of Sir Hartley Shawcross in the House of Commons we are now seeing pretty much eye to eye with the

I should like to explain to
the hon. member for Nanaimo why I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if there were not other ships of countries of the United Nations and the British commonwealth sailing from Hong Kong to Macao and Canton. A friend of mine and his wife are at present waiting in Shanghai to be repatriated. They are unable to leave directly from Shanghai due to the blockade by the nationalist government of the mouth of the Whangpoo river. They have two alternatives. They can go overland by way of Nanking, Peking and Tientsin, and take a British ship from there. As an alternative they can go to Canton and be repatriated from Canton to Hong Kong. Under the circumstances it may be a good thing that there are Canadian ships that will be able to repatriate, not only Canadian citizens and British subjects, but other nationals who have been unfortunate enough to be caught in communist China.

speechtext: I have one brief suggestion to make to the Prime Minister. At the present time we have no minister or charge d'affaires in Austria, and I should like the Prime Minister to give this some consideration. There is no country in Europe that offers such extraordinarily valuable grounds for the supply of information, and this is particularly true of Vienna. I realize that we have not signed a formal peace treaty with Austria when we have done so with western Germany, and there are probably difficulties in the way, but I do believe it would be worth while for Canada to be represented there.

agreement, may I say that the matter is receiving and will continue to receive careful attention. It was well for the
Prime Minister to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Nanaimo for having brought up this matter, and it seems more than a coincidence that since it was brought up an announcement has been made by Sir Hartley

Shawcross respecting the denial of further exports of a strategic nature to Canton from Hong Kong. However, one other matter which was mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo deserves attention. In this issue of Foreign Trade appears an item which refers to the fact that on May 21 the S. S. Chien Men resumed passenger service between Hong Kong and Canton. Then it goes on to say that Ming Sung vessels have been running a weekly service to Canton and ferrying Malayan-Chinese repatriates to the mainland. Certainly those who are being repatriated in those ships flying the Canadian ensign with the maple leaf on it are in fact communists returning to communist China; otherwise they would not be repatriated. I should like to ask the Prime Minister what is going to be done with a view to ensuring that ships flying the Canadian flag will not in fact be used to carry communists back to communist China.
There is something mysterious about the two other ships. The other day the parliamentary assistant stated that there were nine ships altogether comprising the ships built in Canadian yards and turned over to China. Two disappeared under communist control. Five are carrying the Canadian ensign, and we have never been able to find out, or at least it has not been clearly stated, what has happened to the other two.

Supply-External Affairs having Canadian registry. Is that correct?

speechtext: The security for payment of the $12 million was nine ships. The Prime Minister says two of the ships have passed in the night, no one knows where.

subtopic: USE OF WORD IN EXTERNAL AFFAIRS PRESS RELEASE
speechtext: Very well; these two ships passed out of sight, and no one knows where they are. Therefore my submission, by way of a suggestion to the Prime Minister, is that once the security was reduced to the extent of two of the nine ships, there was then actually such a default as would permit the seizure of those ships when in the port of Hong Kong. Aside from carrying communists and potential war materials to China, the Prime Minister admits that these ships are being used in a way which might put Canada in a very difficult position internationally if they were fired upon. That being so, I suggest to the Prime Minister that when these ships come into the port of Hong Kong, there having been, as between the Ming Sung company and the other party to the contract, the government of Canada, such a default as would permit seizure, that seizure should be carried out. After all, the security was nine ships. Today it is seven. No one knows where the other two are. Certainly such seizure could not possibly cause any international repercussions that could be foreseen at the moment, for after all the Ming Sung company specifically asked that its ships should fly the Canadian flag.

When the committee rose at one o'clock we were dealing with the item of administration in respect of the taxation division; and I think various members were competing for the honour of having income tax inspectors visit rural constituencies. In order that there may be no misunderstanding, may I say that there are relatively as many income tax inspectors visiting in the east as in the west. There are two matters that I should like to draw to his attention. One of them is more or less national in scope, covering various parts of Canada, and one is something which I presume is simply local affecting my own constituency.
In December of last year, according to returns filed, the pay and allowances of the armed forces were increased. As to pay, of course no question can be raised. However, as to the increased allowances, I understand the matter is dealt with in two ways. Those members of the armed forces who were living in private homes-in other words, who were living away from the stations or the bases- received; the allowances in cash. Those who were living on the bases, in homes which have been built by the Department of National Defence, did not receive the increased cash allowances. Their rentals or charges-call them what you will-for those homes were increased by the exact amount of the increase in their allowances. The net result was this. I have the table, but it is already on Hansard, and we will not take time to put it on record again. If a man received an increase in allowances of $10, a corresponding charge was made against him for rental. The net result was that he of course received no additional money whatsoever. Yet the Department of National Revenue has assessed him for income tax on this increased allowance. The net result, of course, is that there are thousands of members of the armed forces resident in Canada who, from a financial standpoint, are worse off after they received the allowance than they were before. What I mean is that the allowance was taken by the Department of National Defence as rental and yet the Department of National Revenue charged them income tax on those allowances.
The theory, of course, was that possibly private rentals were going up and if the man was living in a private home for which he had

been paying rent, he would have to use that increased allowance to pay the rent. That may have been true in some cases but as a matter of fact, I know of cases in my own constituency where we happen to have based the army, the air force and the navy, where men of all three arms of the service were paying less rental privately than they were being charged on the base or in the camp, as the case might be, and having received the allowance, they made by it; whereas many in the camp or the base have had their rentals increased and they were charged income tax thereon. I would not say that I have received protests from members of the armed forces because, of course, members of the armed forces are not in touch with members of parliament, and should not be. Nevertheless, I think it is a fair statement to make that the members of the armed forces feel that this action has been rather unfair in that there has been publicity given to the fact that their allowances have been increased whereas, as a matter of fact, they are worse off financially now than they were before. I do not know whether this matter has been brought to the attention of the minister previously, but I would suggest that he should give it careful consideration, and that where these increased charges are made for homes, deductions should not be made at the same time for income tax purposes.
The other matter to which I wish to draw the minister's attention is probably a purely local one, because it probably does not apply in other constituencies in Canada. As hon. members of the committee know-and as a matter of fact, there is an item in the estimates for it-this government and other governments have made payments for the pulling out of apple trees owned by fruit growers in the Annapolis valley. I have not checked these facts myself, and I am speaking now entirely from hearsay. The other matter to which I directed the minister's attention I have knowledge of because I have checked the records. I am informed that farmers in the valley have been assessed tax on moneys received for the pulling out of these trees; in other words, it has been treated as income. Well, I am quite sure that it has never been brought to the minister's attention, but I cannot believe that any responsible officer here would treat money received for the pulling of fruit trees as income, when, as a matter of fact, it is a very small compensation for the loss these farmers have suffered through having to destroy these trees. If you own mining stock, or even Canadian Pacific Railway stock, you are allowed depreciation. You are
Supply-National Revenue allowed depreciation on all sorts of assets. Here are farmers whose whole orchards have been destroyed, have been pulled out. I am told by responsible farmers, and I believe it, that local officials of the department have been treating this money as income. I simply bring it to the minister's attention. I do not expect that he can deal with it definitely this afternoon; but I am stating that as a matter of elementary law, in no way, shape or form can that money be considered as income. I am quite certain that, having brought it to the attention of the department, they will see that in future no further assessments are made in that particular form with respect to money which is simply a small capital payment which goes toward recompensing these farmers for capital assets that have been destroyed.

There are some aspects of several of these items that are normal in character, though questions will be asked in regard to the amounts requested; but with respect to at least one, if not two, of 80709-312
Supply-National Revenue these items there are questions of departure from the principles that have been in effect hitherto governing the provision by parliament of moneys for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Two of these items are to be found in the supplementary estimates, 670 and 671. Item 671 is simply an addition to the provision made for the international shortwave broadcasting station, but item 670 raises important questions of a rather novel nature. That is the item which comes to us following the announcement by the Prime Minister in the house ten days ago that out of the report of the Massey royal commission on arts, letters and sciences, the government proposes to deal with two matters at the present session. This is one of those two matters. May I say at once that with respect to the other matter arising out of the commission report, namely assistance to the universities of this country, I am sure there will be unanimous support in this house.
Item 670 presents this difficulty. The report of the Massey commission is a document of very great importance, and I do not think we will do justice to the importance of that report or of the field assigned to that royal commission for study if an attempt is made to break it up for study piecemeal. I submit there should be an attempt on the part of parliament to view the report as a whole; and at an appropriate stage of the proceedings in the fall session I should think the government would make provision for a debate on the report in general. That in turn, in my submission, should be followed as far as the chapters of the report concerning radio broadcasting and television are concerned by a reference of those chapters to a special committee on radio broadcasting.
In my view it is regrettable that on this final day of this part of the session we should be asked to provide a sum of money which raises some of the fundamental questions dealt with in the report of the royal commission, in effect compelling us to take out some of the chapters of that report and deal with them in piecemeal fashion. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, even those chapters are not before us in their entirety. This item purports to chop off a portion of the recommendations of the royal commission even out of those special chapters to which I have referred. I cannot imagine a more unsatisfactory way of approaching consideration of the important and far-reaching report of the Massey commission. I do not think this method does justice to the report or to the labours of the commissioners.
I said a question of principle was raised here. That question involves policy on the part of parliament and its relations with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I believe

Supply-National Revenue the special committee on radio broadcasting should be set up at the earliest possible date in the fall session, and I suggest to the minister that an item such as 670 could well wait until the fall and until a special committee has been appointed, has studied the report and heard representations concerning it.
It must be borne in mind that the royal commission was not unanimous in its recommendations with respect to the control and operation of radio broadcasting and television. A very weighty minority report was submitted by a distinguished member of the royal commission, Dr. Arthur Surveyer of Montreal, and I should think a parliamentary committee would wish to study the reasons which impelled Dr. Surveyer to write that report. I should think also that such a committee would wish also to hear the views of those likely to be affected by any course which will be involved in the implementation of the recommendations of the majority of that commission.
In that connection we should bear in mind that the last time we had a special committee of this house on radio broadcasting was during the regular session of 1950, and that in turn was the first since 1947. The 1950 committee did not attempt a complete and comprehensive survey of the field of broadcasting. At that time the Massey commission was sitting, and it was felt by all members of the committee that at that stage there was no point in undertaking to duplicate the work of the commission, and, therefore, that the sensible course was to await the report of the commission. Then presumably the committee would be reappointed and invited to study the recommendations contained in the report, and to hear those who wished to make representations in regard thereto. At that time also it was expected that the report of the royal commission would be received very shortly. As a matter of fact during the last debate on radio broadcasting in this house, held on June 28, 1950, at page 4319 of Hansard for that date the Minister of National Revenue said: "I feel that sometime this fall the commission will bring in a report." Therefore the special committee did not attempt to study the system of control and regulation in the field of broadcasting.
The items under discussion, principally 670, do not raise questions as to all the recommendations contained in the report of the royal commission. Nevertheless it seems to me this vote goes to the root of some of the most important recommendations, and I urge the minister that this item should not be proceeded with now but might very well

wait until the fall, when there will be opportunity for a committee to sit and review the recommendations contained in the report. Those who will be affected by many of those recommendations, namely the operators of private broadcasting stations, have not been heard by a committee of the house since 1947. They were not invited to come before the 1950 committee because the committee decided to keep out of that field and narrow its studies down to some other matters principally affecting the immediate financial problem of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. So much, sir, for questions of policy involved in a vote on these items, principally No. 670. I think that kind of decision should be postponed, and that we should not be biting this off piecemeal.
I now turn to the question of finance, and I am trying to make my remarks brief, having regard to the fact that we are all under some pressure at this late stage of the session. The amount that is mentioned in item No. 670, and which is very briefly described, is the sum of $1,500,000 to provide for an interim grant to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation pending amendment of the Canadian Broadcasting Act. Presumably that refers to an amendment that is to come before the fall session of the house; and in providing this sum in contemplation of an amendment that we do not know anything about as yet-and there is not a member of the house apart from the government who knows what is to be the principle or the effect of that amendment-it seems to me that we are being invited as a house to commit ourselves in advance to a principle, and are being invited to take a leap in the dark.
I would ask you to note, sir, if you will, that this item uses the expression "interim grant". I ask you to note particularly the word "grant". This is a new departure. Hitherto the funds placed by parliament at the disposal of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for capital purposes have been by way of loan. Section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act so stipulates. That rule has been followed for years. Now, in the dark, we are being invited to make a grant. It is no longer a loan, but is a grant. We are being invited to make an outright grant of $1,500,000. We are invited to commit ourselves in that way to a departure in principle from the scheme that has prevailed hitherto under the Canadian Broadcasting Act. I submit, sir, that if there is to be a departure of that kind it should be taken only after parliament has had the fullest opportunity of seeing the problem as a whole and of weighing all aspects of it, and after a special committee of

the house has made a detailed study of the problem, and has heard any who may wish to make submissions to it.
Presumably this grant is to be made to provide against the possibility of a deficit in the current operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Lacking any statement in the item itself we can only come to that conclusion. In passing, I must express my protest against items being put before parliament in this sketchy and nebulous form. We are simply left to guess at what is to be the purpose of the vote in the form of a grant of $1,500,000. Why does the item not spell out the particular purpose to which the money is to be devoted? Here we are being invited to legislate. This is one of those items which, in effect, put parliament in a position of legislating, notwithstanding the provisions of statutes and, in particular, section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act.

speechtext: That is what the Prime Minister said he would put a stop to.
