speechtext:
We thought an end had been put to that. That is what we hoped last year. But there is nothing in this item which stipulates the purpose for which the money is to be used. I can only conclude, Mr. Chairman -basing my conclusion on facts quite outside the terms of the estimates-that it is to assist the corporation in meeting a deficit in this year's operations. On that assumption-and on that assumption alone-may I offer a word or two concerning the financial position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I am sure that all hon. members of the committee are aware of the difficulties that the corporation has faced. Its costs have been rising. They have been rising quite rapidly, as was inevitable. The officials of the corporation told the committee that sat at the 1950 session that it was faced with the choice of making a curtailment in services or seeking new sources of revenue. In the fiscal year 1948-49 the corporation sustained a deficit of $43,000. That was not a cash deficit, because there is provision set up for depreciation in the balance sheet of the corporation. In the fiscal year 1949-50 the deficit was $243,000. As to the following fiscal year, we were told a year ago that the deficit was estimated at $962,000 at the beginning of the fiscal year. What we did last year, on the motion of the government, was to vote $650,000 as an advance to the corporation. I would ask that it be borne in mind that that was not a grant; it was an advance to the corporation which was designed to provide for the entire estimated 80709-3124
Supply-National Revenue deficit of the corporation for the fiscal year 1950-51, less the sum set up in the balance sheet for depreciation.
That was the first time that parliament had made a direct advance to meet a deficit on current operations. Up till that time the sums provided by parliament by way of loans had been available for capital purposes. If the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is to face deficits, how are those deficits to be met? That, sir, is a question of great importance. In the light of the recommendations of the Massey royal commission it is a question that is worthy of the best attention of parliament, and it is certainly worthy of the most intensive study on the part of a special committee of parliament. But we are being invited now to vote $1,500,000 for what purpose we know not.
We have had this year, in the house, no review of the finances of the corporation. We have had no review of its operations. We have not had any budget of the corporation laid before us. The report of the corporation for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951, is not before us. It has not been received. I made inquiry at the distribution office as late as noon today to see if, by any chance, the report had been received there. But the report has not been received. The last report that the house has on the operations of the corporation is that for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1950-in other words, fifteen months ago. The report is normally dated about the middle of June, and I can only assume that printing has delayed the submission of the report to the house. But I emphasize again, sir, that in dealing with an important question, a substantial item involving departures from the principles that have been in effect hitherto, the committee has nothing before it of a budget for the corporation and has not before it any report for any period beyond a date fifteen months ago. I wish it to be noted that, in saying that, I am not being critical of the corporation, sir. Let me make that point quite clear. But I am citing these facts as reasons why parliament should not be asked, in these dying minutes of this session, to vote this sum involving, as it does, departures from the principles that have been in effect hitherto. This matter can be just as well dealt with in the fall. The vote of money can be provided then by parliament after it has made a thorough and comprehensive study of the whole matter.
As to ways in which any deficit of the C.B.C. is to be financed, might I make just this comment. I do not wish to launch into a debate on the report of the Massey commission for I do not think this is the time

Supply-National Revenue for it. But may I point out that the commission rejects one of the suggestions that the corporation made to it as to a way in which the deficit could be met. Mr. Dunton made it quite clear to the special committee that sat in the 1950 session that this was not necessarily the only means to which the corporation was committing itself in making the suggestion to the royal commission. It was a way indicated by him in giving testimony on behalf of the corporation before the royal commission as to the manner by which the deficit could be met, namely, by increasing the licence fee from $2.50 to $5. That has been wisely rejected, but I remind hon. members that in the estimates of the Department of Transport the house is already making a substantial contribution, in excess of $600,000, to the corporation by the expedient of collecting, without charge to the corporation, the present $2.50 licence fee.
The cost of that collection is, as I have said, over $600,000. The cost of collecting the fees actually is over 12 per cent on the average of the fees. This very high percentage of cost has been commented on more than once. It is also referred to in the report of the Massey royal commission at page 294.
One other item here is deserving of special mention, namely, item 564, a sum of $1,500,000 which is, you will notice, set out in some degree of detail, and in that respect provides a striking contrast with the nebulous and terse treatment of item 6V0. Here we have a lengthy description of the purpose to which the loan of $1,500,000 to the corporation is put. It reads:
Loans to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation repayable with interest at a rate to be fixed by the governor in council on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine and to be applied in payment of expenditures to cover capital costs of television installations and to support the development of the service. Such loans, with interest, shall be a charge on the revenues of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation next after the charge imposed under the provisions of section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936.
There, sir, you have a clear statement as to the purposes to which this sum of $1,500,000 may be devoted. You have limits fixed as to the use to which this money can be put and you have also the clear proof that it is no departure in principle, but rather a recognition of the fact that it is to be subject to the provisions of section 17 of the act.
This subject of television, sir, Is an important subject in itself. Last year the house provided a loan of $4,500,000 to the corporation to permit it to embark upon extensive expenditures on installations of television stations, two in Montreal and one in Toronto, and at these stations to provide facilities for broadcasting television programs.

This subject of television is increasing in importance all the time, sir. The Massey royal commission estimated when it wrote its report that there are 25,000 television sets in Canada, and the prodigious rate of increase is reflected in statements issued by the dominion bureau of statistics in recent months as to sales. The daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of June 19 says this with respect to sales in the month of March of this year:
Producers' sales of television sets in the month totalled 5,428, more than five times as large as last year's March sales of 926, and the value at list prices rose to $3,250,663 from $391,735. In the January-March period, 13,757 units were sold at a value of $7,593,953 as compared with 2,445 at $1,009,104 in the same months last year.
Sir, these figures indicate the immensity of the problem and the prodigious rate at which the field of television is opening up in Canada. Here again, sir, in the report of the Massey commission we have an important and weighty minority report written by Dr. Arthur Surveyer. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this vote of $1,500,000 is not so urgent that it could not wait until the fall session, until there has been an opportunity to review the whole subject and deal with it in a comprehensive and not just a piecemeal manner.
True, this item, 564, was inserted in the main estimates before the report of the Massey commission was received, but, sir, it seems to me that the terms of the report make it evident now that if we are to do justice to that report, and the important recommendations that it contains, this item ought, like the other item to which I have referred, No. 670, to await that comprehensive study which is not possible at this session, but will be possible, we trust, at the fall session of the house. In the meantime, this additional vote of $1,500,000 is simply apparently to be a further endorsement of the type of operation that the corporation announced previously.
We thought we were going to have actual Canadian television programs by September 1 of this year. Reports now indicate that there have been delays, and the corporation will not be able to commence its operation- until probably as late as next spring. In the meantime, private applicants for channels for the purpose of television broadcasting are simply being left in the air. These applications have been left in a frozen condition for the last 2J years. Action is required, Mr. Chairman, but action after we have seen the problem whole, and the committee is the only body that can do that. In the meantime we are committing ourselves in effect to the expansion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation

television program and we have no opportunity now of reviewing the whole report of the commission and of dealing with these other important aspects of the control and operation of television in Canada that are urgently crying for study and action. In that respect I refer particularly to these applications on the part of private applicants who have been waiting for 2J years for an opportunity to risk their own money in providing television in Canada, and have been delayed in doing so by the paternalistic attitude on the part of the corporation.
In conclusion, let me say again that departures in principle are involved in vote 670. A new path is being followed, and in advance of our having given in this house even superficial study to the report of the Massey royal commission. There is nothing so urgent about the item that it could not wait until the fall. Parliament can provide whatever money parliament at that time thinks it necessary to provide for the needs of the corporation during the whole fiscal year, because the fiscal year runs until March 31, 1952. Nobody is going to be prejudiced, I submit, Mr. Chairman, by allowing this matter to stand until parliament can deal with it in a proper, comprehensive and statesmanlike manner.

I repudiate that suggestion entirely. It is too important a matter to be carried without discussion. There are many points we should discuss, and I am sorry it is so late in the session that it may not be possible to have as long a discussion as we might otherwise have. However, that is not my fault.
The hon. member for Eglinton has pointed out that this debate resolves itself pretty much into a matter of dealing with the C.B.C. national service, with the international service, and with television. As all hon. members are aware, this whole matter of broadcasting, whether it be sound broadcasting or video, has been the subject of debate, representations and a report by the Massey commission. That report was received only within the last ten days or two weeks. The hon. member for Eglinton has placed special stress on that report. I am sorry he saw fit to base his whole argument upon the minority report.
May I review briefly the subject matters he has taken up. I shall start with the national service, and the $1,500,000 by way of an interim grant to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, pending an amendment to the act. This is entirely an interim measure, and it is to enable the C.B.C. to meet its bills, pending decision in the fall with respect to legislation regarding revised revenue arrangements for the corporation. We understand that it is entirely different from a loan.
Let me say here that this is the first time in the history of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation when it has asked for a grant rather than for a loan. All financing of the C.B.C. has been done on the basis of loans which have been or will be repayable. The C.B.C. is the property of the radio listeners and licence payers of the Dominion of Canada rather than of the government of Canada; and it is for that purpose that the C.B.C. is responsible to parliament rather than to the government.
As hon. members understand, it is run entirely by a commission or a corporation which is independent of the government, and my position is that I report from the corporation to parliament and to the government. At the present time the corporation is in a strained financial position. This situation arises from the general increase in cost levels in Canada over the last twelve years. The corporation has been caught by these rising costs, while the basis of its revenue has remained unchanged.

Supply-National Revenue
The main part of the revenue of the corporation comes from receiver licence fees. The level has been, as hon. members know, $2.50; and that has not been changed since 1938. Meantime, as everyone knows, costs of operation of all kinds in Canada have risen greatly. It has been estitnated that costs of the corporation have more than doubled in the last twelve years. At the same time the rates on its main revenue have remained the same. Obviously no organization can continue to function with rising levels of expenditures and a stationary rate of income.
The C.B.C. has made its position clear on a number of occasions, particularly to parliamentary committees, and to the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences.
The hon. member for Eglinton complained that there has not been a meeting of the parliamentary committee on the C.B.C. for a long time. That is explained by the fact that this commission was sitting.

The situation however is such that the corporation just has to have some additional funds to carry on during the coming months. The annual report of the corporation for the year 1950-51 is not yet available. indicate however that the over-all deficit for last year will be something in the neighbourhood of $1,272,000 after depreciation.

That is the fiscal year, and that is after depreciation. The over-all operating deficit before depreciation, in the national sound service, without taking into account preliminary current expenditures on television, will be $913,000. Of this amount $650,000 was covered by a loan to the corporation approved by parliament last year. The remainder comes out of C.B.C. resources, thus further reducing the working capital.
During the year the corporation operated on the principle of maintaining services at current levels, and carrying out its commitments, but not of introducing extensions or improvements involving increased expenditures. That practice was laid down at the last meeting of the parliamentary committee. That last meeting examined the position with reference to finances, and recommended specifically that, pending consideration of a new revenue basis for the system, the corporation should be enabled to maintain its present standard of services. That was the recommendation of the committee.
The government extended a year ago a $650,000 loan based upon that recommendation to meet the deficit for the year ending 1951. The chief addition to the coverage of the system during the year was a station at Windsor, and that had been started some time previously.
Arrangements were also made for relay transmitters in points in northwestern Ontario and British Columbia where service was badly needed. Increasing costs to maintain services and meet commitments, however, led to the deficit I have mentioned.
This year the corporation again faces still higher costs with little expectation for higher revenues on the present basis. It has estimated that the gap between revenues on the current rate and expenditures necessary to maintain present services will be over $2 million. It would have been possible in theory to have met the situation by a reduction in its services. The reductions, however, would have been such that they would have changed the whole national broadcasting service as we know it now. It should be pointed out however that this is the first time that a straight grant of funds has been requested for the C.B.C. Up until last year the C.B.C. had met any deficit it had out of its own resources. Last year assistance was provided by means of a loan, which is still an obligation on the corporation. I think

it should be pointed out that under the broadcasting act the C.B.C. has been expected to build up its capital assets out of its surplus revenues. It has in fact operated up to this time on that basis.
I think hon. members will agree that in principle it is undesirable to make grants to the C.B.C. for operating expenditures. I agree with them. There should be laid down a system of revenue for the corporation adequate for it to carry on a proper national broadcasting service in Canada under existing economic conditions. Just as with any other well-run enterprise the corporation should then have the responsibility of carrying out its task with the maximum efficiency within the limits of the revenue provided.
This vote asked for today is to prevent wholesale dislocation of the broadcasting services pending a full consideration of the royal commission report and possible legislation. At the fall session of parliament the house may wish to examine this whole question of financial provision for the national broadcasting system.
Frankly I admit that the government has not had time or the opportunity to give the study to the Massey report that we wish to give it, and we have not had time to formulate a policy or legislation based upon the report if we should accept it. I think it is quite likely the report will be accepted. I have made some study of it and I think it is a splendid report. I am not going to go into the details with reference to the arguments on that report. We had on that commission some of the most learned gentlemen in Canada and as a result of great study and the representations which have been made to them they have seen fit to make recommendations with reference to the future conduct and carrying on of the system.
Let me turn for a moment to the loan of $1,500,000 for television. This is a further loan to the C.B.C. for the development of television. At the end of 1949 parliament approved a loan of $4,500,000 to the corporation to enable it to establish television production centres in Montreal and Toronto. I think hon. gentlemen will remember that at that time I told the house that further loans would be necessary, probably up to $10 million. I realized fully at that time that the introduction of television into Canada was going to be a far more costly proposition than was generally regarded in this country. There was a demand for it and in order to keep up with the developments throughout the world and on this continent it was thought
Supply-National Revenue fit that we should proceed with the development of television on a fairly restricted basis.
The first loan covered the capital costs of the two centres. This new loan of $1,500,000 will cover mainly preliminary work and current costs during the first months of operations. It is really an operational loan rather than a loan for capital expenditures, but in that would be included some capital equipment.
The corporation had planned to have these centres in both cities operating in September of this year. However, unforeseen difficulties have been encountered. Delays in obtaining some construction materials are holding back the studio and transmitter building in Toronto. In addition, word has recently been received that there will be a delay of some months in delivery of television studio equipment on order from Great Britain because of defence pressures there. Orders totalling about $1 million were given for equipment to the Marconi people. We were pressed in this house to give that order to Britain so that they might have Canadian and United States dollars with which to make purchases of food in this country. As a consequence of the delays that have occurred it does not appear as though the Toronto centre could be operating before late winter of 1952. The actual date still depends on deliveries of construction materials and equipment from Great Britain.
The situation in Montreal is that the studio building is well advanced but there has been a considerable delay in starting the transmitter building and tower on Mount Royal. This was due to lack of permission to go ahead on the Mount Royal site. The necessary approval has been given recently and work has begun. It is expected that it should take about a year to complete the transmitter and the tower installations on Mount Royal.
These two centres have been planned as the first keystones of a Canadian national television system. It is planned that programs from them would be transmitted, not only directly in the Montreal and Toronto areas but also later over stations to be developed in other areas. Programs would be supplied to stations in other parts of Canada, for some time at least, by means of kinescope recordings.
In the fall, following consideration of the Massey report, decisions can be taken regarding revenue arrangements for the television system and plans for its extension in other parts of the country. I recommend again the Massey report and particularly that section of it which deals with television. Applications have been made by private

Supply-National Revenue companies to get television airways and allocations. The report recommends that they be not proceeded with until our own two stations reach a further stage of development.
Let me say a word with reference to the international service, and I am not going to be much longer. This service continues its work, the main purpose of which is the projection of a clear picture of the life of Canada and a definite attempt to combat in every way possible communistic ideology. During the past three years many changes have come about in the policy or controlling philosophy of the international service.
It continues to speak to many countries where the battle for men's minds is not carried on with intensity and in a friendly manner. This is true, for instance, of the broadcasts to the United Kingdom, other commonwealth countries, the Latin American countries and the Scandinavian countries. But where the conflict of ideologies is really sharp and dangerous to the cause of freedom as we understand it, as in Italy, Germany, Czechoslovakia and Russia, the "Voice of Canada" has played a very definite combative role through its transmissions. May I quote a passage from an article by H. B. Hodson which appeared in a recent issue of the BBC Quarterly, where he says:
The problem of propaganda by radio is highly controversial, and I do not propose to embark on it here, beyond asserting three propositions.
He then goes on to detail the influence of propaganda. The international service has continued to expand and consolidate its transmissions. In February, 1951, broadcasts to Russia were inaugurated. These broadcasts are daily, two in number of one-half hour each. The Italian service has been consolidated and is now meeting with great success. In fact, for the first three months of 1951 the mail from Italian listeners was larger than the mail from any other European country to which we broadcast. The actual number of letters received in three months was 4,075. We now have a weekly program to Finland and this has met with a surprisingly successful response.
The policy governing the C.B.C. international service continues to be worked out through careful consultation and co-operation between the responsible officials of the international service and the Department of External Affairs.
There are many arguments for further expansion of the service. Pressure has been exerted in favour of our embarking on broadcasts to Russia in Ukrainian, to Czechoslovakia with more extensive use of Slovak, to Poland, to Yugoslavia, to Hungary, etc. Forceful reasons are advanced in favour
of all these proposed extensions. At the present time, however, the facilities provided for the C.B.C. international service are taxed to their capacity. In other words, all the available good listening time for European transmissions is occupied at present and no expansion such as has been suggested can be undertaken without serious curtailment of the present service. Two additional transmitters would be needed for further additions to European services.
The general response to the international service continues to be very good. During the year 1950 the total number of letters received from listeners in all parts of the world was 41,147. I am not going to bore the committee with details of all that has been done by the international service. We have copies of many of the letters written by people who express great satisfaction at having heard the C.B.C. signal.
In spite of the fact that additional European services in Russian and Finnish have been developed the operating budget of the C.B.C. international service remains at approximately the same level at which it was a year ago. This fact will necessitate the most stringent economy in many aspects of the service, notably in its publications and in keeping adequate personnel which is necessary if the service is to maintain the position it has built up.
The greatest vindication that there could be of the policies that have been in operation over the past ten or twelve years so far as the C.B.C. is concerned is found, in my opinion, in the Massey report. At this time I am not going to attempt to make an analysis or deal critically with the minority report. However, I say, after having looked over it, that the Massey commission, which had the opportunity and the time to hear representations from all classes and kinds of people and organizations in Canada, has embodied in their written report vindication of the policies that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has developed and put into effect ever since its inception.

I take this opportunity to pay my tribute to the officials of the C.B.C. I hope they will not let any pin pricks bother them throughout the year but will carry on happily.

When I spoke earlier I
indicated the difficulties that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is facing as the result of rising costs. Of course to maintain its services, let alone expand them, it has to have adequate revenue. That is self-evident. The. whole question that presents itself at this stage is where that additional revenue is coming from and on what terms. Hitherto the revenue has consisted of the $2.50 licence fee, and last year some $650,000 advanced by way of a loan.
The minister has said quite frankly that the government has not yet had time to study the Massey report nor, as he put it, time to formulate a policy. Those are words of the highest significance for the purposes of this debate and certainly with relation to the argument I have put before the committee. My whole submission today is based upon the fact that nobody in this house has yet had an opportunity to formulate his ideas on policy adequately after sufficient study of this report. The government is no exception to that rule. The minister has said that the government has not had time to formulate a policy. Yet in the face of that admission the government is asking the house to approve a departure from the policy that has prevailed from the time of the inception of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation right down to this minute.
The minister referred to that in his opening remarks and said that the funds that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had received from parliament had always been received by way of loans. Quite so, Mr. Chairman. That is why when one comes to examine an item like No. 670 one is struck at once by the fact that here is involved a complete departure from that principle which is written into the terms of section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, and has been faithfully followed from the time this corporation came into existence, as I have said, right down to this minute. Notwithstanding that fact, notwithstanding also the 80709-313
Supply-National Revenue fact that the minister admits that the government has not had time to study this report and has not had time to formulate a policy, the government is asking the house to take a jump in the dark and to depart from that recognized, established, statutory policy.
If I needed any further vindication of the submission I have made to the committee this afternoon, it is contained abundantly in the statement the minister has made today. I urge the committee to give the Massey commission report the thorough study it deserves, not to take a superficial glance at it and then some slapdash ill-considered action following submission of the report, or to make a departure in policy without a comprehensive study of the whole situation. What I am asking now is that this item should be allowed to stand until the kind of study that the importance of this report justifies and demands is given to it, and that no departure from established and statutory policy should be made until the house has studied the report, and until a committee of the house has gone exhaustively into all aspects of the report in relation to broadcasting and television.
No harm will come to the corporation by deferring the voting of these sums until the fall, because we will be able in the fall to do everything that is required in the way of voting money to provide whatever assistance the corporation needs during the fiscal year, which will run until the 31st March next. We will be able to do it then with all the knowledge that ought to be possessed and which is not, in my submission, in the minds of the government, in the mind of the minister, or in the minds of members sitting in this committee today. It seems to me only simple common sense that we should defer action until we study this question, that we should not make an important departure from established policy in the face of the inadequate consideration that has been given hitherto. No harm would come to the C.B.C. by waiting until the fall session for that necessary study. This means of making a grant to the C.B.C. may not be the means that parliament will decide is proper to provide the needed revenues for the corporation to avoid deficits.
There is nothing that the minister has said today that commits him or commits the government to the acceptance of that method as the method by which deficits on the part of C.B.C. are to be met in the future with the nuisance $2.50 licence fee continuing. Therefore I say that we are not doing justice to the report of the Massey commission, we are not doing justice to the importance of this problem, we are not doing justice to our own

Supply-National Revenue claim to common sense by proceeding today to vote these sums involving a new departure in policy and based on the most superficial consideration of a problem of the highest importance for all Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot for the life of me see where we are doing an injustice to the Massey report by agreeing to provide an interim grant to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Nor do I see why a particular brand of common sense demands that this item should be deferred until the fall. Surely the situation is that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been running deficits for some years, and it has again this year. If the corporation is on its toes, as we expect it to be, it must be planning its winter programs now, and it cannot plan them very successfully if it knows it is not going to have any money to carry out those programs. Therefore if we expect the sort of programming from the C.B.C. that we have had in the past it has got to be certain it will have some interim grant such as this. So I differ with the hon. member for Eglinton; I say it is common sense to let the corporation know that part of the money is available to it now.
I agree with the hon. member that it would be a good idea to have a special committee on broadcasting in the fall. We had such a committee last year. For once the Canadian Association of Broadcasters was not represented, so we could spend all our time examining thoroughly and meticulously what the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was doing and what it was hoping to do. We investigated it to the exclusion of all other agencies. We investigated charges of extravagance, incompetence and loose management, and the corporation came out of that investigation very well indeed. I do not think the fact that the royal commission was sitting at the time hindered any member of that committee or prevented him asking the questions he had in mind. That fact may have had some effect upon the report finally submitted, but beyond that I will disagree with my hon. friend. At that time the C.B.C. got the sort of going over it should get more frequently. In the past I think at times the committees may have wasted time listening to the complaints of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. However, if they wish to appear when the next committee is set up no one will welcome their appearance more than I. Of this I am certain; the C.A.B. certainly will not completely adopt the minority recommendations in the Massey report. Indeed, if there is one thing of which I hold the C.B.C. culpable 
it is that it has not lived up to its own regulations. If we had this independent authority which has been asked for over both the C.B.C. and the C.A.B., I think the private broadcasters in this country would get the shock of their lives. If there is to be a committee set up in the fall I want it to be told that the C.B.C. has lived up to the regulations concerning private radio stations more than has been the case in the past. I have no objection to private radio stations; I think they have an invaluable part to play as community stations; but we must not forget that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a national institution, and I hope the government will see its way clear to implement the recommendations of the Massey commission and give the C.B.C. the funds it needs to do the job we expect from it.

I do not think this day should go by or this item should pass without saying a word or two on it, as the expression of my own mind after giving these matters a good deal of thought. I am going to follow the same tack I have followed a good many times before; perhaps hon. members know what that is.
I am still not satisfied that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in its talks department, is being operated in the interests of the Canadian people and our concept of our free way of life. I know that the very moment one speaks in that vein the cry goes up that one is attempting to break down public confidence in this great national institution. I have no desire to do that, but when I have a conviction I am not going to remain silent. If I have to choose between warning of what I believe to be the dangers on the path along which I think we are being very subtly led, and taking a chance on being branded as one who is destroying public confidence in the C.B.C., then I am afraid I shall have to choose the latter and take that chance. I would not say this if I had not listened to these talks occasionally; and of course it may be said that I just happened to listen to the wrong talks. No citizen sits with his ear glued to the radio from early morning until late at night and takes in every talk that goes over the air. I am not a radio fiend; I do not do that. It is impossible for me to say that I have listened to every talk on the C.B.C. programs. I have not. But I have received a number of complaints from people who think as I do. I do not mean to say they think as I do about the C.B.C., but think as I do about life, as I think in respect to the enemy of our democracy that is out to destroy us if possible, and

as I think along certain Christian lines. I have had these complaints verbally and by correspondence.
I know what the answer is. The answer is: Well, we have our talks department and we attempt to call in speakers who will give us a broad range of views. These men hold different views concerning this matter and that, and we believe in free speech. That is the cry. When the corporation is asked about that very often they will say this is a principle that has been adopted and favoured by parliamentary committees that have sat in the past. Of course that statement contains only an element of truth. If it comes to a question of free speech what parliamentary committee will not say it is in agreement with that principle? Of course it will. We are all in favour of free speech. But let me say that we do not have free speech when we have a talks department responsible for choosing the people who use the national network to put over their views. You cannot have free speech by that process. The only way you can have free speech is to have the air open to everyone. I realize that is neither practical nor possible, but let us not put up the cry that we are in favour of free speech and are doing our best to give the people every possible view of a situation. I say that when we take that attitude we are taking the attitude that the people are incapable of making up their own minds. It is all very well to say: We have our publications, we have our newspapers; would you say the same thing about them? Any newspaper or any periodical that wishes to express its views is welcome to do so. Any individual in the country who wishes to express his view is welcome to do so. But when we are using the taxpayers' money for the purpose of a talks department which chooses the speakers, I say we have no right to do that. That is my conviction.
In pursuing my argument, I would ask this question: As to the news of the day, the news of the week or the happenings in any part of the world, is it necessary to have that news pre-digested by half a dozen, a dozen, or a hundred people and then to have it expounded over the air to be redigested by the people? Is that necessary? I say it is not. I say that it is not a healthy procedure. For instance, such topics as the MacArthur incident have been commented on. Broadcasts have been given on it. Speakers have been chosen to express their views. I say I do not agree that anyone else should use this publicly-owned institution to pre-digest that news and put it over the air-excuse the expression "put 80709-313J
Supply-National Revenue it over"; I do not mean it in any derogatory sense-or expounded over the air with their own particular mental slant upon it.

What I believe, Mr. Chairman, is that the talks department of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is becoming a propaganda panel and is being used to condition the mentality of our people to accept, at least without great protest, a way of life that is contrary to that which we hold dear and which would otherwise lead us on to the destiny which free peoples have envisioned. I agree that there have been some excellent speakers. I know that someone will say: Oh yes, the excellent speakers are those who agree with you. I know that is something that will be said. It is not a matter of agreeing with me. These things cannot always be

The corporation is asking for money. I am not going to say that they should not be given assistance when they need it. But here is one place where they could cut down a little on expenses. I do not believe it would hurt this country one tiny, little bit if they simply cut out completely their talks department. As a matter of fact, I believe that the country would be better off for it.

Supply-National Revenue invariably-I was going to say invariably, because I believe that is so-persons who were teaching in those institutions mentioned the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and how they listened to the objective presentation of the news over the C.B.C. I found that quite a large number listened to the ten o'clock broadcast at night.
I think all hon. members will agree that that is usually an objective presentation of the news of the day, both national and international. There are times when perhaps those of us who are interested in what happens in this house may feel that there are some deficiencies in the news. We regret that. Coming down to the item of $1,500,000 suggested as a grant to the C.B.C., my view is that the House of Commons would be warranted in adapting the proposal and supporting the granting of this amount to the corporation. I am not going into all the phases of the Massey report; but anyone who reads it will see at once that while there are some criticisms of the corporation, there is a great deal of praise for much that it has done. It has brought good music, good opera and good drama into the homes of the Canadian people. Its literary critics have recommended good books and good reading to the people of

Some of us in this chamber now were in New York at the meeting of the United Nations last autumn, at which time we installed a television set in our delegation lounge, with the thought that we and our staff would enjoy it. I think the consensus however was that the sponsored programs we were seeing were, in the main, below the level we would expect from this great new organ of public entertainment and information. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke of the degrading of television in the United States by advertising, but that difficulty could easily be met by proper controls, and those proper controls could be achieved by setting up a semi-judicial board to decide on such questions. I just want to bring two matters to the attention of the minister under this item. First I want to congratulate the minister and the officials of his department on their earnest endeavour to try to improve conditions in the fishing industry. There are, however, two things that I should like to bring to his attention while the fisheries estimates are under discussion. One of them is this, and I realize that there are few fish dealers who will agree with the statement I am going to make. There is a great spread between the prices that are paid fishermen and the prices that the consumers are being forced to pay in this country today. There are many glaring examples of unreasonable prices being charged for fish at a time when meat prices are high and when the fishing industry might have come into the place

Supply-Fisheries
that we would wish to see it. For instance, last year in the county that I represent, pollack-which is an extremely fine fish and is caught in great quantities in that county- was sold for as little as one-half cent a pound. I do not mean that just a few hundred pounds were sold at that price. Tons and tons were sold for half a cent a pound, and a cent a pound was considered a good price. All during the winter months they were asking 17 and 18 cents a pound for that same fish in the dry state. Now ground fish, cod, is being sold at 2J cents a pound, which we had to fight for. It takes about 3 pounds of cod to make a pound of fillets. I noticed in the Ottawa paper just a night or two ago that cod fillets were 47 cents a pound in the city of Ottawa. The fishermen did not get more than 7 cents or 8 cents for that pound of fillet. Who got the spread of 600 per cent and 700 per cent between the price that the fishermen received and the price that the consumers were obliged to pay? There is something wrong somewhere. There is something wrong in our organization. I would think that it might be well to investigate this matter. I do believe the spread is too great. I do not believe there is any reasonable excuse for it.
The price of meat during the last two years has been the highest of any time in the world's history. That period would have been a very fine time for the fishing industry to have put their products into the homes of the Canadian people, where we might have been able to keep them when meats were cheaper again. But the price that the consumers are obliged to pay has prohibited in many, many cases any great demand for fish.
There is just one other item that I shall speak on briefly because I realize the committee is getting weary and wants to get home. The Department of Fisheries has given great assistance to the maritime provinces, and I believe to other parts of Canada, in connection with small draggers and equipment for the fishermen to use in order that they might increase their production. With that idea I am not quarrelling at all. I think it is a fine idea, but if after the fish are caught markets cannot be found it does not bring about the results that we would like to have. In the particular section I spoke of where these fish were sold last summer at J cent and 1 cent a pound, fishermen were allowed to fish only about two days a week. There was no market for the fish three days a week. The catch at that time was quite good. They could have made a very fine living, but there was no market. I have tried to convince the department which

works through the provincial government, that young men-I do not mean young men without experience in the fishing industry, but young men with extensive experience in the fishing industry who have asked for financial assistance to establish fish curing plants-should be given assistance. I have brought this matter to the attention of the department which, as I say, works through the provincial government, and I have not been able to get any financial assistance for these men, many of whom I know personally. I have worked with them on the water for many, many years. They know how to cure fish and they know how to market them after they are cured.
There is one case-I will not mention any names-of two young men who have been in the industry for 25 or 30 years. This past winter they put every dollar they had into a fish curing plant. When the plant is completed they will be short of funds to cure their fish this summer. In the salt fish industry it means that you must have several thousand dollars to carry on because your catch will not be sold until the coming winter. I have not been able to get any financial assistance for them.
I do not want to give the impression that I am criticizing the assistance given to the small draggers. With that I agree. But at the same time, increasing their catch, if markets cannot be found, will not help the situation. I do believe that men of experience, who are reliable, and need assistance to get established in the fishing industry should have every bit of encouragement this department can give, financially and otherwise.

There is just one thing I should like to say with regard to these post office items. I refer to the dropping of the term "royal mail". I do so because the Post Office Department is a government service. It carries the King's cipher, George Rex, and the arms, which are the royal arms of Canada because they bear the crown, the symbol of the monarchy. I raise this matter for another reason. Nobody is more keen on his Canadianism than I am, but the more I travel, the more I see of other countries on this earth, the more I appreciate the fact that we have a parliamentary system of government whose head is a monarch, the King. When an offence is committed against the laws of this country the accused is charged and the charge is "Rex v. John Doe". It is not "Canada v. John Doe". It is not the republican form, "The people v. John Doe". It is Rex v. John Doe. I feel that the dropping of the prefix "royal" is a regrettable and a retrograde step.
I say this in all sincerity because it is not helping our Canadian nationalism. We as Canadians have a peculiar nationalism. We are not republicans and we are not colonials. We have a country of our own, our own parliament and our own king. Those things are things that we are very proud of and things which we should treasure and cherish. The dropping of the word "royal" is not very ii portant in some ways, but I consider it is t) imendously important because it is a symptom not of a great and growing Canadianism but of an inferiority complex that resents the King perhaps because he is an Englishman and lives in London. I say this in all sincerity and not to criticize anything in the Canada post office, but I would sincerely ask the Postmaster General to consider calling the department the Royal Canadian Post Office. I understand there is the Royal Australian Post Office and the Royal New

Zealand Post Office, and I feel that the dropping of the prefix "royal" does not aid us. In fact it belittles our stature as a free and independent nation.
With that in mind I sincerely ask the Postmaster General to give the matter consideration. I say this as a Canadian of the fifth generation, a Canadian on both sides of my family, and I ask that we retain the prefix "royal" with regard to all our federal services, whether it be the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force, or anything else. It should be the King's Royal Mail.

I could have gone along myself with the word "empire", but I was very glad to accept the word "commonwealth" because I knew there were many Canadians who disliked the word "empire". But I had believed, until the last few days, that there was one thing perhaps above all others in this country on which we had a common view, and that was with regard to the crown. I have heard that said again and again, and I have never heard it denied. I thought that was one thing where, in spite of all our differences, we could- and when I say "we" I mean largely the people of the two original races in this country-meet	and where differences
disappear. I think that was true of Laurier and it was true of Borden. It was true of Mr. King.

And as I implied a moment ago, to me-and I lived for some years in the province of Quebec-when I saw the words "Poste Royale" on the mail vans and letter-boxes-it was frequently to be seen-it was one of the signs that, well, here is something that does not divide us, where we can unite.

But it did not seem too important to me that it was being done, and incidentally I do not know how it was done. I want to come back to that in a moment. It seemed to me it was being done by a rather-what shall I say-narrow view but I said to myself again: I am not going to complain about that because it is pretty hard to make an argument. I have feelings about it, but I am not going to say anything about it and I never did. But now we come to this which, as I say, has seemed to me to be the one, perhaps the greatest thing, which we had in common, and we need things in common. Now is this going to disappear too?

Mr. Chairman, this is the first item under the group headed "standards division". I should like to ask the minister whether attention has been given by his department to the possibility of setting up standards in two particular fields. I refer on the one hand to the sizing of clothing, and of women's and children's clothing in particular; and I refer on the other hand to the fibre content of clothing.
I have in my hand a document that has probably been placed in the hands of other hon. members, namely a bulletin from the Canadian association of consumers, in which this matter is dealt with rather fully. I find that housewives and women across the country in particular remember the experience that they had during world war II when, under the auspices of the wartime prices and trade board, certain standards were established. Women, when they purchased clothes in those days, felt that they had some guarantee as to the value they were getting for the prices that were paid. Well, that all went out the window when the wartime prices and trade board ceased to operate, and there is a very real problem.
I understand from this document and from other sources, that some work on the setting up of standards, as to the sizes of women's and children's clothing, has been done in the United States. I understand that the results of that research are available to this country. But it would seem that what is needed is some direction from the government. The same is true with respect to the quality of fabrics from which clothing is made. We now have so many different kinds of fabric, and although the store clerks try to be helpful in telling the average purchaser what the particular item of clothing is made of so far as its material is concerned, there is no guarantee. There is no label that is proof to the purchaser as to the fibre content of these various fabrics.
I have in mind the Canada standard trademark that we approved by a bill that went through parliament two or three years ago. I have in mind other ways and means by which the Department of Trade and Commerce does set up standards. One obstacle would be that usually a grain elevator requires a flour-milling industry, and the sale of offals to a livestock population which, in Newfoundland, I understand is not very great. subtopic: USE OF WORD IN EXTERNAL AFFAIRS PRESS RELEASE
speechtext: This item is for $50,000,000 and a similar amount appeared in the main estimates. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: USE OF WORD IN EXTERNAL AFFAIRS PRESS RELEASE
speechtext: The commitments to date for capital assistance amount to approximately $113,000,000. That amount will not be required this year, but it was felt that an additional $50,000,000 should be provided to take care of the commitments during the present fiscal year. I have explained before that where capital assistance is given the facility created remains the property of the crown. It must be built on land owned by the crown and the asset created is the property of the crown. The recovery will depend on the ability of the crown to dispose of the property after the emergency. I think I stated that after the last war the average recovery was something between 60 and 65 per cent.

subtopic: USE OF WORD IN EXTERNAL AFFAIRS PRESS RELEASE

subtopic: USE OF WORD IN EXTERNAL AFFAIRS PRESS RELEASE
speechtext:

It is all subject to treasury board cost auditing and is also subject to renegotiation after the actual costs are determined.

I should like to say just a few words. I could say more but I will not at this time. First of all, I want to say that I was pleased to note the expression of protest by the hon. member for Hamilton West when she learned how wage rates at the printing bureau tend to lag behind the going wage for printing in cities like Hamilton and Toronto, as well as in Ottawa and Montreal. I feel that the time is long overdue for a revision of that part of the Public Printing and Stationery Act which lays down the principle governing the wage rates at the printing bureau. I have not the act in front of me so I cannot quote it, but the gist of the appropriate section is that the wage rates paid at the bureau shall not be greater than the wage rates paid in Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.
That leads the printers working at the bureau to feel that there is supposed to be some relationship between the two sets of wages referred to. Actually there is no need for the provision that the wage rates shall not be greater than they are in those, other cities because they are always less. The practice is to review them from time to time in the same way all prevailing rates are reviewed, namely, by reference to the Department of Labour, but there is always a time lag. The increase that is given to the printers at the bureau is always the increase won by the printers working in Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal six months or a year earlier, or sometimes a little less, even at that. I feel strongly that that part of the Public Printing and Stationery Act should be overhauled and it should be laid down as a principle that the wage rates at the bureau are to be on a par with the current wage rates in the three cities mentioned.
The usual tendency is to compare them with the wage rates paid in job shops in the three cities named in the act, but I feel, particularly when parliament is sitting, that the job of producing Hansard is more akin to work in a newspaper shop. I would point out that the scale of wages in a newspaper shop is always higher than in job shops.
There are two other things I want to say and I shall express myself as briefly as pos-

sible and serve notice on the Secretary of State that I will be back in future sessions with these points. Despite the plausible answer he gave a few weeks ago I feel that not only should the government permit employees in places like the printing bureau to belong to trade unions of their choice, but they should enter into collective bargaining with those employees through the trade unions of their choice.
I feel also that the government should pay more attention to the shops with which printing is placed to see that as much as possible, if not all of it, is placed with trade union shops. A short while ago I placed some questions on the order paper seeking information as to the volume of printing done at the bureau and the volume let out to other firms. Then with respect to printing let out to other firms I asked what percentage was given to union shops and what percentage to non-union shops. The answer that came back was that no information was available on that point.
Then I placed another set of questions asking for details as to the particular shops to which printing was let in each of the last three complete years and I asked which of those shops were entitled to use the trade union label of an allied printing trades council. While I got information as to the shops with which printing had been placed and the dollar value thereof, with regard to the union label question I was told that no information was available. I may tell the Secretary of State that I have taken steps to ascertain for him the total dollar value of this printing in the three years in question that was let to shops that could use the trade union label and the total dollar value let to shops not entitled to use the trade union label. Since the Secretary of State was not able to give me that information I shall give it to him either this fall or in the 1952 session, and I shall again press my point that government printing should be done in union shops.
